newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Racist violence tags spread of Nazi music in Sweden.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Racist violence tags spread of Nazi music in Sweden.

text.p: Head shaved, black costume adorned with Nazi SS symbols, the lead singer of Swedish rock band Svastika spits hatred from the stage.
"We are the masters. White aggression," he screams into the crowd of gyrating teenagers.
Security guards hired by the concert organisers man the door. No one without the right credentials is allowed in and anyone causing trouble inside is thrown out.
The aim seems to be to ensure no unwanted attention is drawn to the gig.
"They think if no one knows they are there then no one will notice as the numbers of neo-Nazis climb across Sweden," said Inspector Greger Wahlgren of the Swedish police.
BANDS ARE TIP OF NEO-NAZI ICEBERG
Svastika is one of more than 40 neo-Nazi or white power bands that have emerged in Sweden over the past two years.

They are the visible tip of a growing iceberg of neo-Nazism which has in recent years turned Sweden into the "big brother" of right-wing extremism in the Nordic region and been accompanied by a frightening upsurge of racist violence.

Police monitoring the rise of the movement estimate there is at least one neo-Nazi concert a month in Sweden, attracting up to 100 people, and bigger events, attended by up to 1,000, about five times a year.
With names like True Blood, Steelcapped Strength, Storm, Divions, and Odium, white power bands preach against blacks, Jews and homosexuals.
"Hey nigger, we're ready when you are," run the lyrics of one song, for which a 26-year-old distributor from southern Sweden faces charges of making threats against minority groups.
Somalia Kickers was named after band members attacked and kicked two Somalis in a country town.
Wahlgren, who is coordinating a national policy to fight racism, said it had been virtually impossible to stop the dramatic rise in the number neo-Nazi bands.
Concerts are organised in secret and hard to trace. Organisers book several venues for the same night. Concertgoers meet in one place and are taken to the chosen spot.

The bands' CDs, believed to be manufactured in Taiwan, are not sold through shops but only through mail-order networks advertised in right-wing extremist publications, such as Sweden's Nordland magazine, or at white power concerts.
"Up to 5,000 copies of these records are being sold each month," Wahlgren told Reuters in an interview.
MUSIC ATTRACTS YOUNG TO EXTREMIST CAUSE

"I think Nazi music has played a very important role in this rising tide of neo-Nazism. Before they tried to get members by speaking, by papers, but you don't attract young people just by talking. Music works."
An investigation by the London-based Institute for Jewish Policy Research found the level of neo-Nazism in Sweden was unusually and worryingly high.
"The neo-Nazi elements have found effective means of establishing a racist sub-culture which has seen remarkable growth in the past years," the institute said in its 1996 Anti-Semitism World Report.

"In fact not since the war has Swedish neo-Nazism been as self-confident as it is now. The level and quantity of propaganda relative to the total population (of 8.8 million) is unique in an international perspective."
Neo-Nazi groups boast an estimated 1,000 hard-core members and several thousand sympathisers.
SURGE IN RACIST CRIME
More frightening still is the accompanying dramatic rise in racist crimes.
In 1994 police investigated about 1,000 racially-motivated crimes across Sweden. Since then the numbers are known to have risen. Latest figures will be released early next year.
Anders Tegstrom, a police researcher preparing Sweden's first major study into racist crime, said the worst crime in 1995 was the murder of 14-year-old Jan Hroon, son of a Czech immigrant.
Jan was kicked to death by three skinheads after they tried to make him pledge allegiance to the neo-Nazi cause. His body was dumped in the sea. His murderers were convicted and jailed.
SKINHEADS OF 1980S THE TRIGGER
Today's racist sub-culture was triggered by a violent, skinhead movement that emerged in Sweden during the mid-1980s.

In the 1990s, with Sweden for the first time facing rising unemployment, now running at eight percent, right-wing extremists started to attack immigrants who moved to Sweden during the open immigration policy of the 1960s to 1980s.
One in eight people in Sweden is estimated to be of foreign extraction.
Wahlgren said the authorities realised action had to be taken before the neo-Nazi movement grew further and became more organised.
"We've been lucky so far because there are so many organisations and they are not all friends, so they have been unable to link and grow quickly," he said.
"it would be a nightmare if there were one group with one set of leaders. We have to make sure that does not happen."
